answer.exemplar: Differencing replaces each level with the change since the level before it, and because a trend is a steady addition to every level, differencing cancels it: a series climbing by 10 a month becomes a flat line of 10s. That is what makes the series easier to work with, because what is left no longer drifts, so one set of assumptions about behaviour fits the whole history instead of having to change month by month. The cost is the level. A change fixes no starting value, so the two series are related only up to a constant, and that constant cannot be recovered from the differences: add 5 to every original month and the differenced series is identical. Any statement about how much stock is held, what the balance is, or whether a particular month was high has left the data. The discipline is to keep the first recorded level beside the differenced series so the original scale can always be rebuilt, and to say plainly which of the two is the series being forecast.

questions.explanation: Differencing is not a cleanup, it is a change of subject. Each new value is the change since the level before it, and because a trend adds the same amount to every level, taking differences cancels the trend out entirely: a series rising by 10 a month becomes a flat run of 10s, which is far easier to model. What is cancelled is also the level, because a change fixes no starting value, so a hundred different sets of levels produce exactly the same differences. Every question about how much is held, what the balance is, or whether one named month was high has to be answered from the original series, which is why keeping the first level beside the differences is not bookkeeping but the only way back to them.
questions.hint: Ask what a single change tells you about the two months it connects.

answer.exemplar: The deciding question is what the quantity is, not how the chart should look. A count of events is consumed as it happens: vehicles cross a gate, a request arrives, a ticket is raised, and each one happens exactly once in exactly one interval. Those quantities have no meaningful zero inside the day, so two of them add and the daily total is the honest roll-up, while averaging them answers a question nobody asked and understates the volume by a factor equal to the number of intervals. A level behaves the opposite way. A temperature, a queue depth or a balance is held over the interval rather than spent, and two of them added together mean nothing, so the mean is the only defensible roll-up and the extremes are worth reporting beside it because a mean hides them. The trap is that the same averaging code is often applied to a whole row of columns without anyone asking which kind each one is, so a defensible implementation carries the roll-up rule with the field definition, making the decision once when the field is declared rather than rediscovering it in every report that touches the data.

questions.explanation: The test is whether the quantity is consumed or held. Events are consumed: a vehicle crosses the gate once and is not crossing it again, so two hourly counts are two disjoint sets and adding them is the only way to describe the day. Levels are held: a temperature at 09:00 and a temperature at 10:00 are not two temperatures, they are one temperature observed twice, and adding them produces a number with no meaning at all. Averaging counts understates a day by a factor equal to the number of intervals, and summing levels invents a total. The tempting shortcut is to apply one roll-up across a whole row of columns, which hides both errors behind a single tidy figure.
questions.hint: Ask whether two of the hourly values could both be true at once.
questions.learningObjective: explain the test that selects the correct roll-up

answer.exemplar: The chart mixes two kinds of object unless the hole is marked. Twenty-nine positions hold measurements: the instrument spoke at those times and the values are what it reported. A thirtieth position filled by interpolation holds an estimate the instrument never made, produced entirely by assuming the quantity moved in a straight line between two points that were measured. Drawn identically, the two are indistinguishable on the chart, so a reader counting spikes, fitting a trend or setting an alarm threshold will treat the estimate as an observation without ever knowing it was one. The assumption is not unreasonable in itself, since a temperature that rose steadily before the gap and rose steadily after it probably did move smoothly through the night, but the cases that matter most are exactly the ones where it could not be: a freezer that failed, a meter that was swapped, a shift change that took the output to zero. A gap is a statement that something was not known, which is a fact about the run, while a filled value is a statement that it was known, which is not. The right output keeps the hole visible, states the rule used, and lets whoever reads the chart decide whether a smooth series may be estimated and a discontinuous one may not.

questions.explanation: The chart ends up holding two different kinds of object that look the same. Twenty-nine positions are measurements the instrument actually reported; the thirtieth is an estimate produced entirely by assuming a straight path between two points that were measured. Once both are drawn identically, a later reader counting spikes, fitting a trend or setting an alarm cannot tell which is which, and will treat the estimate as an observation. Interpolation is a reasonable estimate only when the quantity moves smoothly through the gap, and the cases that matter most are the ones where it might not: a failure, a meter swap, a shift change to zero. A gap is a fact about the run, while a filled value is a claim about it.

answer.exemplar: Events per day is a ratio whose denominator is a unit of time, so it answers a question about pace, and pace is not the same thing as whether a service is working. A service carrying five times the demand can handle five times the events, be slower on every one of them, and still show the larger daily figure, because the denominator grew along with the numerator. The comparison also depends on the day, since a weekday rate and a weekend rate are different quantities under the same name and a figure averaged across both describes a day that may never occur. A fair comparison states what its rate is a rate of, and it does that by pairing the count with the demand it was asked to serve: requests per request offered, faults per thousand attempts, or resolution time against a stated target each tie the numerator to something the service was responsible for and can be read without knowing how busy the period was. Where a rate is kept at all, the underlying counts belong beside it and the units named, because a per-day figure chosen to flatter one service and penalise another is a presentational choice rather than a measurement.

questions.explanation: The denominator is the whole claim. Events per day divides a count by time, so a service with five times the demand can handle five times the events, be slower on every one, and still show the larger figure, because the denominator grew alongside the numerator. The unit also hides which day is being described, since a weekday rate and a weekend rate are different quantities wearing the same name. A defensible comparison ties the numerator to the demand the service was asked to serve, such as faults per thousand attempts, so the figure can be read without knowing how busy the period was. Where a per-day rate is kept, the underlying counts belong beside it, because a unit chosen to flatter one service and penalise another is a presentational choice rather than a measurement.
